According to the conjectures in~\cite{barnett2008stability}, which have recently been proved~\cite{kangro2010convergence}, this guarantees exponential convergence.
nodes.statement_short: Enclosing the Laplace singularity hull with Helmholtz sources encloses the Helmholtz singularities and thus gives exponential convergence.
assumptions: locating the Helmholtz sources so that they enclose the convex hull of singularities of the Laplace problem
conclusions: guarantees that all of the singularities of the Helmholtz problem are enclosed

nodes.statement:

As explained in Section~ef{sec:poleReloc}, we seek a rational function $P/Q$ that approximates $\widehat{W}$, and we do so by solving weighted linear least-squares problems of the from~\eqref{eq:minProbIRF}. To avoid the trivial solution, a normalization condition, to be specified below, must be imposed on one of the polynomials. otag \ \mathbf{\widehat{Q}} &= 	ext{diag}\left[\widehat{Q}(z_1), \widehat{Q}(z_2), \ldots, \widehat{Q}(z_K)ight],

nodes.name: Discretize the weighted fitting norm
nodes.statement: Using the quadrature rules of Section~\ref{ssec:quadForIRF}, we discretize the continuous norm in~\eqref{eq:minProbIRF} and write the minimization problem as, \begin{equation} \min_{\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}} \, \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{n=0}^N{ \dfrac{\sqrt{\lambda_k}}{\widehat{Q}(z_k)}\left|{b_n z_k^n - a_n z_k^n \widehat{W}(z_k) }\right|} \end{equation} in which the unknowns are the monomial coefficients of $P(z)$ and $Q(z)$, denoted $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{a}$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Replace the continuous norm by a quadrature sum over monomial coefficients.

nodes.name: Build two orthonormal bases by Arnoldi iteration
nodes.statement: To deal with this problem, we construct two orthonormal bases, one for the column space of $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{\Lambda}^\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{\widehat{Q}}^{-1}\mathbf{V}$ and one for the column space of $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{\Lambda}^\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{\widehat{Q}}^{-1}\mathbf{\widehat{W}V}$. This can be done with the Arnoldi iteration~\cite{arnoldi1951principle,saad2003iterative}, by noting that the columns of $\mathbf{A}$ form a Krylov subspace, \begin{equation} K= \text{span}[\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{Z}\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{Z}^2\mathbf{d}, \ldots, \mathbf{Z}^N\mathbf{d}], \end{equation} where $\mathbf{Z} = \mathrm{diag}\left(z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_K\right)$ and $\mathbf{d} = \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{\Lambda}^\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{\widehat{Q}}^{-1})$, and similarly for the columns of $\mathbf{B}$.
nodes.statement_short: Orthonormalize the two Krylov column spaces with Arnoldi to fix the conditioning.

nodes.name: Rewrite in the new basis and normalize
nodes.statement: we rewrite~\eqref{eq:irfDiscrete} in the new basis, \begin{equation} \min_{\mathbf{\tilde{c}}} \, \left|\left|\left[\mathbf{P}, -\mathbf{Q}\right]\mathbf{\tilde{c}}\right|\right|, \end{equation} and impose the normalization condition $\tilde{c}_{2N} = 1$, which corresponds to $Q(z)$ being monic in the new basis.
nodes.statement_short: Recast the minimization in the orthonormal bases and make $Q$ monic there.

nodes.name: Solve the over-determined system in the least-squares sense
nodes.statement: The solution of the minimization problem is then obtained by solving the over-determined linear system \begin{equation} [\mathbf{P},-\mathbf{Q}_{1:N-1}]\mathbf{\tilde{c}} = \mathbf{Q}_N \end{equation} in the least-squares sense.
nodes.statement_short: Least-squares solve for the coefficients in the orthonormal bases.

nodes.name: Recover the new poles from a generalized companion matrix
nodes.statement: They are the eigenvalues of a generalized companion matrix~\cite{coelho1999robust}, \begin{equation} \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{H}_{1:N,1:N} - H_{N+1,N}\,\mathbf{\tilde{c}}_{N+1:2N}\,\mathbf{e}_N^T, \end{equation} where $\mathbf{e}_N$ is the $N^\text{th}$ column of the order-$N$ identity matrix and $\mathbf{H}$ is the upper Hessenberg matrix obtained from the Arnoldi iteration used to generate the orthonormal basis for colsp($\mathbf{B}$).
nodes.statement_short: Return the zeros of $Q$ as eigenvalues of a Hessenberg-based companion matrix.

nodes.name: Cauchy-theorem criterion for a pole being inside $D$
nodes.statement: When a pole is close to the boundary, or the boundary shape is complicated, it may be nontrivial to find out whether a pole is inside $D$ or not. By restricting ourselves to boundaries described by piecewise rational functions, a solution to this problem is readily obtained. Using Cauchy's theorem, a pole $z'$ is inside $D$ if and only if \begin{equation} \int_C \dfrac{1}{z-z'}dz = \int_0^1 \dfrac{1}{z(s)-z'}\dfrac{dz(s)}{ds} \,ds = 2\pi i \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: A pole lies inside the domain exactly when the winding integral of $1/(z-z')$ around the boundary equals $2\pi i$.
assumptions: boundaries described by piecewise rational functions
conclusions: is inside $D$ if and only if $\int_C \dfrac{1}{z-z'}dz = \int_0^1 \dfrac{1}{z(s)-z'}\dfrac{dz(s)}{ds} \,ds = 2\pi i$

nodes.name: Analytic evaluation of the pole-location integral
nodes.statement: This integral cannot be calculated exactly using the rational Gauss-Chebyshev rules because the Chebyshev weight function is absent. However, it can be calculated analytically by breaking it up into rational-function sections, writing the integrands as rational functions, and using a partial-fraction expansion.
nodes.statement_short: The winding integral is evaluated exactly by partial fractions over the rational boundary sections rather than by quadrature.
